lesson.title: The Errors That Wait Until Your Code Is Actually Running
lesson.summary: A runtime error occurs in code that is perfectly valid Python, when a line tries to do something impossible given the actual data at that moment, such as dividing by zero or reading past the end of a list.
lesson.body:
A runtime error, also called an exception, is fundamentally different from a syntax error, even though beginners often lump the two together as "the program isn't working." Where a syntax error means the code itself is not valid Python, a runtime error means the code is valid Python. Python's parser has no complaint about it at all, and the program actually starts running normally. The failure happens later, when some specific line, executing with some specific data, tries to do something that turns out to be impossible right then, and Python halts the program at that exact line and prints a traceback describing what went wrong and where.

The single most important thing to understand about runtime errors is that they depend on data, not on how the code is written. The exact same line of code can succeed on one run and fail on another, depending on what values happen to flow through it: dividing by a variable that happens to equal zero this time, looking up a list index that happens to be out of range for this particular list, or opening a file that happens not to exist this time. Here is an example using indexing.

```python
scores = [92, 78, 85]
print(scores[5])
```

Running this prints a traceback whose final line is:

```
IndexError: list index out of range
```

There is nothing grammatically wrong with scores[5]; square-bracket indexing on a list is completely valid Python syntax. The problem only exists at the moment this line actually executes, because the list scores has just three elements, at indices 0, 1, and 2, so index 5 does not point at anything. If scores held six or more elements instead, this exact same line would run without any error at all. That is the signature of a runtime error: it depends on run time conditions, the actual state of the data when the line executes, which is also why it is called a runtime error.

Python has many built-in exception types for different kinds of impossible situations encountered during execution: ZeroDivisionError for dividing by zero, IndexError as seen here, KeyError for looking up a missing dictionary key, NameError for using a variable that was never defined, FileNotFoundError for opening a path that does not exist, and many more, including TypeError and ValueError, which get their own dedicated chapters later because beginners so often confuse them. Every one of these shares the same core quality that distinguishes runtime errors from the other two categories: the code is valid and starts running, but a specific line, faced with the specific data at hand, cannot do what it was asked to do.
